topic: How Unsloth's new computer-use beta on one consumer GPU stacks up against metered cloud agents from OpenAI and Anthropic on what a screen-driving agent actually costs you.
title: Unsloth computer use vs cloud agents: what your GPU really replaces
description:
Unsloth computer use vs cloud agents, priced rung by rung.
OpenAI caps its ChatGPT agent at 40 messages a month on Plus, and Anthropic bills every screenshot as image input. On your own card, the best-rated open screen model is about 19 GB once, and QLoRA fine-tuning fits in 22 GB of VRAM. This video climbs the full comparison: the meter, the memory, and the weights.
You'll learn a one-line rule for deciding when one consumer GPU replaces a metered cloud agent.
Subscribe for weekly local AI builds. (Narration is AI-generated.)

narration_full: The meter says forty messages a month. Your GPU has no meter. You've got a gaming card, and you've watched Claude and ChatGPT drive screens for a fee. Teaching one yourself doesn't take a datacenter. The meter is the first thing you pay. OpenAI caps its ChatGPT agent at forty messages a month on Plus, then folds it into ChatGPT Work. Hit the cap and the agent stops. Your side has no meter. Unsloth just shipped a computer-use beta, an agent that reads your screen and clicks with your approval. It ships off by default, under permission rules you set. Then there's what running it costs. Anthropic's computer use tool bills every screenshot it reads as image input. The agent looks, and the meter ticks. Long tasks look a lot. Your side downloads once. The best-rated open screen model is a GGUF, a packed file that runs on your own hardware. It takes about nineteen gigabytes of memory, vision file included. After that, looking is free. Using it feels like a new hire leaning over your shoulder. It sees only the screen, it moves your mouse, and it asks before it clicks. Unlike a hire, it re-reads every screenshot from scratch, so long jobs can drift. The full job needs twenty-two gigabytes of VRAM, your card's own memory, at minimum. And the add-on is yours to keep. MiniMax's new image model is the proof. Its weights download, and this week's Unsloth release trains them. The full job needs twenty-two gigabytes of VRAM, your card's own memory, at minimum. And the add-on is yours to keep. One honest catch. It's a beta, and it behaves like one. In Unsloth's own test, two of six runs misread the screen or quit. It only drives apps on your own machine. The meter, the memory, the weights. Rent the rare jobs to the cloud. Run the routine ones on your own GPU, with Unsloth.
